beats.narration: It proves that science without an understanding of the archaic is blind. And because Dracula gets that invitation into the asylum, he gains access to Mina, which leads to the most devastating
attack in the book, but also the most brilliant counterattack. Picture this. Two things of different size side by side.
On one side, the vast churning expanse of the Black Sea. Hundreds of miles of open, chaotic water. And on the other side, pinning all of that infinite space down, is a small,
ticking gold pocket watch held in an old man's hand. The infinite chaotic space of Dracula's escape route is pinned down by the precise mechanism of Victorian timekeeping and hypnosis.
Dracula realizes he's losing the war in London. His boxes are being sterilized by the heroes.
He's cut off from his biological assets. So in retaliation, he attacks Mina.
He breaks into her room and he forces her to drink his blood from a wound in his chest. It's a horrifying violating
He tells her, "You are now to me flesh of my flesh, blood of my blood, kin of my kin, my bountiful wine press for a while, and shall be later on my companion and
my helper." He establishes a psychic tether to her. It's an invasive surveillance technique.
By forcing her to ingest his blood, he marks her. He turns her into a transmitting device, hoping to spy on the group's plans through her mind. But Van Heling, the brilliant synthesizer
of the ancient and the modern, turns the tables. He realizes that the tether goes both ways.
If Dracula can see through Mina, Mina can see through Dracula. But there is a What's the catch?
The vampire is bound by the strict rules of nature. He can only change his form or exercise his supernatural powers at specific times,
at dawn, at noon, or at dusk. So, Van Helsing pulls out his gold pocket watch. Yes. The ultimate symbol of modern standardized timekeeping. He uses his watch to time
the exact precise moment of dawn and dusk. And at those moments, he hypnotizes Mina.
Now, we should note that in 1897, hypnosis or mesmeriism was transitioning from a parlor trick to a legitimate psychiatric tool.
Right. Van Helsson uses it to drop Mina into a trance, an eaves drop on Dracula's sensory feed. She goes into this trance and reports exactly what Dracula is experiencing.
I can hear the waves lapping against the ship and the water rushing by. Canvas and cordage strain and masts and yards creek. They reverse the vampire's invasive
surveillance into military reconnaissance. They weaponize the biological tether against him using timed psychological analysis. Dracula thinks he has planted a bug in their headquarters, but instead
he has handed them a GPS tracker on his own Exactly. The precision of the pocket watch and the technique of hypnosis overpower the ancient blood curse. They know he is fleeing back
to Transylvania on a ship, which triggers the final sequence of the book.
And I want you to picture this final contrast. Two things of different sides side by side.
On one side, a slow, heavy, horsedrawn carriage struggling along a snowy riverbank in Eastern Europe. And on the other side, racing past it entirely unseen, is a tiny, invisible
spark of electricity shooting down a telegraph wire. Ancient physical transport is entirely bypassed by the speed of modern communication and steam travel.
Dracula flees London via a ship called the Zarena Catherine, heading back to Varna, the port where he started. He uses his supernatural control over the wind and fog to speed his ship's journey,
hiding inside his very last box of earth. But the heroes don't try to chase him on another sailing ship. They don't try to out sail the weather. They use the infrastructure of the empire.
This is the logistical race across Europe. They pack their weapons, their typewriters, and their documents,
and they head for the train station. They take the Orient Express. They use steam launches and rail connections.
They are bypassing the natural elements entirely through industrialization. And crucially, they use international telegraph lines to track his ship.
Lord God, who is Arthur Holmwood, uses his massive wealth and status to have an agent at Lloyds of London, the massive insurance market, telegraphing him daily shipping reports.
They are receiving telegrams that say Zarina Catherine reported this morning from Dardinell's. They are tracking him in real time without ever having to physically see his ship.
Mina, who earlier in the book called herself the train fiend because she loves studying timetables for fun,

uses her knowledge to plot their interception. Right when they arrive in Varna and find out that Dracula actually bypassed them, using his supernatural influence to steer the ship up the river to the port of Galat instead.
They don't despair. They don't give up. Mina just consults the timets. Van Helsing asks, "When does the next train start for Galat?" And Mina immediately knows at 6:30
tomorrow morning. It is a stunning victory of data over geography. Dracula is essentially trapped in his wooden box, floating up a frozen
